```{r}
library(preJCERBGVAR)
s <- jcer_simulate_gvar(4, 120, seed = 31,
                         variables = c("y", "r_short", "r_long", "price"))
fit <- jcer_bgvar(s$data, s$W, draws = 30, seed = 31)
responses <- paste(rep(c("JP", "EA", "KR"), each = 4),
                   c("y", "r_short", "r_long", "price"), sep = ".")
g <- jcer_irf(fit, "US.r_short", responses, horizon = 8, shock_bp = 25)
```

These are synthetic innovations, not historical causal estimates. Inspect a
single response pair before producing a large research figure:

```{r, fig.height=5}
plot(jcer_irf(fit, "US.r_short", c("JP.r_short", "JP.y"), horizon = 8, shock_bp = 25))
restrictions <- data.frame(variable = c("US.r_short", "US.y"),
                           horizon = c(0L, 1L), sign = c(1, -1))
signed <- jcer_irf_sign(fit, restrictions, "US.r_short", c("JP.r_short", "JP.y"),
                         horizon = 8, max_tries = 5000, seed = 10)
signed$acceptance_rate
plot(signed)
```

`benchmarks/optional_bgvar.R` loads the installed BGVAR example data in a local
environment; no BGVAR data or code are redistributed. Its historical `stir`
variable is a short-term market rate, not the policy decision itself. The
1995Q1--2013Q4 sample is not current 2026 data. Any real-data application needs
explicit transformation, units and credible identifying assumptions.

The main historical validation now uses `benchmarks/run_historical_validation.R`.
It loads `eerData`/`W.trade0012` from the installed package at runtime, takes
the same countries and columns for both methods and explicitly renormalizes
trade weights after country selection. GDP is 100 times the log difference;
Dp is multiplied by 100; rate inputs are explicitly declared decimal and
converted to percent points. The common transformed sample has 75 observations.
No unit is guessed from numerical magnitudes. Country/period/variable/weight
manifests are saved alongside results, without copying observations.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
source("benchmarks/historical-common.R")
d <- historical_data(4, include_long_rate = TRUE, input_rate_unit = "decimal")
baseline <- BGVAR::bgvar(d$data, d$W, draws = 1000, burnin = 1000,
                         prior = "NG", SV = FALSE, eigen = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
# Same inference and country-error GIRF definition; replace post-processing only.
fast <- jcer_irf_bgvar(baseline, "US.stir", c("JP.y", "JP.stir", "JP.ltir"),
                        horizon = 12, shock_size = .25, rate_unit = "percent")
plot(fast)
```

The benchmark compares every retained raw IRF draw and all five quantiles to
`BGVAR::irf()`. Stable-draw sensitivity uses the same filtered draw subset for
both post-processors. Main timing retains all draws to fix the work budget and
reports stable fractions. Timing equivalence does not establish MCMC convergence
or identify a causal policy effect. The separate MNIW comparison aligns the
world-generalized shock definition before discussing model differences.
